content:
The CI of LML now generates a new set of web pages at https://leanmachinelearning.org/LML/exposition/ (not yet linked from the main website). The goal of those pages is to help understand the results and definitions of the library.
The most interesting pages are probably the "details" pages for each declaration, like https://leanmachinelearning.org/LML/exposition/chapter-online/module-online-bandit-algorithms-etc/decl-Bandits___ETC___regret_le/. On that page, we see on top a theorem from LML, and below it we have a list of all definitions needed to understand its statement, and then transitively all definitions and theorems of LML needed to understand the statement and those dependencies, starting from Mathlib.
The goal is that someone can as quickly as possible be convinced that the theorem proves what we claim it does.
One first thing those views highlight is that we need to flesh out the docstrings of the definitions to better explain what they mean.

The website generation code is at github.com/LeanMachineLearning/exposition/, which started as a copy of https://github.com/mattrobball/lean-exposition/ by @Matthew Ballard . It's vibe-coded and needs more testing to check that the dependencies of the results are reported correctly.
It also probably needs many small changes to be more visually pleasing. Feel free to open issues on github.

As a next step, I'd like to generate lean challenge files for all results which import only Mathlib and list all definitions needed from the project to state the theorem, that could be fed to Comparator. It's currently a work in progress. Getting compiling challenges files will also test that the dependencies are correct.

More generally, I'm looking for suggestions of things that we could report to solve the problem of alignment between the formalization and the informal meaning. One such possibility would be to add tags to some definitions or theorems to say that they correspond to some result in a reference book. Another possibility could be to tag results as being part of the important properties of a definition, and report those to check that our def behaves like we expect. There are probably many other ways that I did not think about.

The links with minimal lean files for every declaration are now functional, and compile for all 612 of them (which needed a couple fixes to the way we collect dependencies through notation).
For example, on top of the page showing the regret bound theorem for ETC there is a link "Minimal Lean file" that opens the online editor with a Lean file containing only the dependencies in the project needed to state the theorem.

This is awesome, but also leaves something to be desired... :-)

The dependency graph view is, in my view, essentially useless. Without labels on the nodes / some indication of hierarcy, it's extremely difficult to extract information from.

What I would love to see is under the "Body uses" and "Type uses" drop-downs, a hierarchical tree of the transitive dependencies (deduplicating as needed, ie. don't show the children of anything whose children are already displayed higher up).

This would be even better if there were hovers that popped-up either the doc-string or signature, so we could look at things without jumping to new pages.

(It's possible that some of these trees would be explosively large. Perhaps an automatic "... and 7 more items" that you could click on to reveal more?)
I would love to see these ideas refactored out into reusable tools for any repository eventually. It is great.

I agree about the graph! I copied it from Matt's work and did not think about it at all yet. I mostly worked on getting the dependencies right to get thw detail page cards. A graph with the style of verso-blueprint would be much better.

The tools are already repository agnostic, except for the css of the pages that uses the red theme of LML.
I'm also running it on the Brownian motion project when testing.

On BM about 20 of the 1200 minimal lean files still fail to compile, all because of omitted fields in anonymous structure constructors: those fields are autoparams and automatically proved by fun_prop in the initial code, which does not work anymore in the minimal file. The solution could be to add the fields with sorry proofs but claude did not find a reliable way to do that yet.

But the dependency computation is robust enough to produce 1780 compiling lean files on 1800 test cases. And visual inspection of several of them makes me think that it's not marking too many dependencies either, but that's a less systematic check.
